supplementary_news.content: Log in Log in Forgot Password Close News News Comment Features Obituaries Business Sport Magazine Review Saturday Money Travel Galleries Weather Puzzles Lead story Share Fourth jabs won’t be necessary, say experts JCVI says current boosters are protecting vulnerable as evidence grows of omicron being milder Laura Donnelly Sarah Knapton Simon Johnson FOURTH jabs are not currently needed, the Government’s scientific advisers have said, as evidence grows that omicron is far milder than previous variants. The Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI) announced last night that boosters continued to provide high levels of protection against severe disease from omicron in older adults, including the most vulnerable. 40pc The proportion of people with Covid in Scotland’s hospitals who are being primarily treated for other conditions Its analysis found that three months after receiving a third jab, protection against hospitalisation among over-65s remained at about 90 per cent. Ministers have been exploring the possibility of a fourth jab for several weeks, after Israel, considered a global pioneer in Covid vaccinations, launched such a programme last month. But Prof Wei Shen Lim, the JCVI’s chairman of Covid-19 immunisation, said: “The current data show the booster dose is continuing to provide high levels of protection against severe disease, even for the most vulnerable older age groups. For this reason, the committee has concluded there is no immediate need to introduce a second booster dose, though this will continue to be reviewed.” It came as Covid numbers in Britain fell for a third day in a row and evidence emerged that hospitalisations arising from Covid cases were 12 times lower than during last year’s winter peak. There were 178,250 cases reported in the UK yesterday, down from 179,756 the previous day and a fall of more than 11,000 from the same day last week. Figures from Scotland show that just 1 per cent of people who test positive for Covid are ending up in hospital, down from 12 per cent last January. Meanwhile, figures from England show the number of patients in mechanical ventilation beds has fallen to 728, a decline of 63 in a week and the lowest number since October. During a visit to King’s College Hospital in south London, Sajid Javid, the Health Secretary, said: “When we look at omicron versus the previous variants, of course there are some encouraging signs; we know now that omicron is less severe.” However, Mr Javid emphasised the need for people to come forward for their booster jab, with the NHS facing “challenging times”. On the same visit, Amanda Pritchard, the head of the NHS, said a fortnight of further hospital admissions for Covid-19 was “already baked in”, as some NHS staff faced “the steepest climb of the pandemic yet”. Staff absences because of Covid isolation are continuing to cause severe pressures on services, with warnings that this could continue for some weeks. The JCVI said that rolling out a fourth jab programme “would add to the significant existing operational pressures” for the vaccine rollout and the rest of the NHS, noting that “the current omicron wave is progressing very swiftly, offering limited time for additional vaccine programme measures to have a substantial impact within this wave”. They said that even in the most vulnerable, a fourth jab would provide “limited additional benefit against severe disease at this present time” and that the main aim of the vaccination programme remained prevention of severe disease, not protection against mild or asymptomatic infection. Protecting against all infection would require regular jabs, as often as every three months, which “is not considered a sustainable long-term strategy” the JCVI said. They added that alternative vaccines, including variant-specific jabs, which may become available later this year, may prove better suited to providing long-term protection against novel variants. The comments echo the remarks made earlier this week by Sir Andrew Pollard, the chairman of the JCVI, who told The Daily Telegraph that “more strong evidence is needed” before the rollout of a fourth vaccine. He said: “We can’t vaccinate the planet every four to six months. It’s not sustainable or affordable. In the future, we need to target the vulnerable.” It came amid increasing evidence that omicron is milder than previous variants. Latest figures show an increase in hospitalisations, with 2,434 admissions yesterday, up from 2,080. But NHS data show that in some areas as many as 45 per cent of patients in hospital with Covid were admitted for other reasons. There were 13,045 people included in the official Covid hospital figures by Jan 4, but 4,825 of them had been admitted for other reasons. This means 37 per cent of Covid hospital patients were admitted for other reasons – compared with a figure of 24 per cent earlier this month. The figures show that, in the week ending Jan 4, hospital cases of “incidental Covid” rose by 135 per cent, from 2,065 to 4,845. The number of patients classed as “primarily Covid” saw lower growth, of 83 per cent, from 4,479 to 8,200. The Midlands had the highest proportion of incidental cases, at 45 per cent. In London, the percentage of non-Covid cases included in the figures hit a high of 44.7 per cent on Jan 2 but has since fallen to 38.2 per cent. The latest statistics also show that deaths from Covid in care homes are up to 10 times lower than this time last year even though there have been a greater number of outbreaks. Calculations by The Telegraph also suggest that in England just 2 per cent of cases are ending up in hospital compared with 12 per cent last winter. New data from Public Health Scotland also show that only one in 100 people who recently tested positive for Covid required hospital care, compared with one in eight at the end of January. The Public Health Scotland study found that four in 10 people in Scotland’s hospitals with Covid were being primarily treated for other conditions, rather than being admitted because they required care for the virus, piling pressure on Nicola Sturgeon to scrap her hardline restrictions. Editorial Comment: Britain needs a route back to normality Share Enlarge Coronavirus Share Infected Scots in hospital for other reasons, data show Simon JohnsonScottish Political Editor FOUR in 10 people with Covid in Scotland’s hospitals were primarily admitted for other reasons, according to an official analysis published yesterday. Only 60 per cent of acute hospital admissions involving patients with Covid were determined to be “because of” the virus, a study by Public Health Scotland (PHS) found. This figure was a sharp reduction on the 68 per cent recorded in a previous PHS study covering March to August last year, when the delta variant was the dominant strain. PHS said that it was important to differentiate between patients who were admitted to hospital “because” they required treatment for Covid with those whose admission was “coincident” with testing positive. The agency said this was because “knowing this information can help signal whether population-level changes in public health measures may be warranted, such as a tightening or easing of restrictions”. In another extraordinary finding that raised questions about Nicola Sturgeon’s restrictions, the study said only one in 100 Scots who catch Covid require hospital care after the UK’s vaccination programme and the spread of the milder omicron variant. It found the proportion of people who needed hospital care after getting the virus dropped from 12 per cent in January last year to just 1 per cent in December. When age was taken into account, the report said people were 12.5 more times to be hospitalised with Covid if they are unvaccinated than if they had received a booster or third vaccine dose. Nearly two thirds of confirmed, probable or possible omicron cases (64 per cent) recorded since the start of November were found to have been contracted by the under-40s, who have lower vaccination levels. Despite this, the study said there had been a 31 per cent increase in hospital admissions in Scotland in the week ending Dec 28, with the highest number involving patients aged over 80. The findings were based on an analysis of patient records at NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde and NHS Grampian at the end of December and beginning of January, with both health boards recording “reasonably similar” results. They further increase the pressure on the First Minister over her hardline restrictions in Scotland after she admitted on Wednesday she was rethinking her strategy for tackling Covid thanks to omicron’s increased transmissibility. In a major about-turn that brings her approach more in line with that of Boris Johnson, she disclosed her government will shortly unveil a blueprint for Scotland to live with the virus in the long term that would be “more proportionate and sustainable and less restrictive”. She admitted that using restrictions to tackle the variant were less effective after figures showed the proportion of Scots with the virus doubled from one in 40 to one in 20 over the festive period. This was similar to many areas of England, where no new measures on social distancing, licensed premises and large events were introduced. The UK Government’s Covid dashboard yesterday showed that with 2,079 cases per 100,000 Scotland had a higher rate than England on 1,787. Dr Sandesh Gulhane, a GP and the Scottish Tories’ shadow health secretary, said the PHS report had provided “a crucial missing piece of the puzzle through this pandemic” by disclosing four out of 10 Covid patients were not being treated primarily for the virus. He said: “This is a significant percentage, which could mean the difference between whether restrictions are lifted or increased when it comes to decision time for the Government.” Noting the report covered only two of the largest health board areas, he added: “The SNP must commit to providing the full data, as soon as possible, so that we can make sure our Covid response remains balanced and proportionate in the months ahead.” But Humza Yousaf, the SNP’s Health Secretary, said: “This analysis suggests that Covid-19 continues to increase the pressure on the NHS in Scotland – with the majority of Covid-19 patients admitted to hospital because of the infection and admissions continuing to affect a disproportionately greater number of older people.” Prof Jason Leitch, Scotland’s national clinical director, said patients with Covid imposed an additional burden on the NHS whether they required treatment for the virus or another condition. He said: “A failing transplant is much harder to manage if a patient has a positive Covid test for example.” Prof Linda Bauld, a public health expert who advises the Scottish Government, noted that daily case numbers will become less relevant as positive lateral flow tests no longer need a PCR confirmation. However, the PHS research also disclosed that Scotland’s troubled Test and Protect contacting tracing system was failing to complete a growing proportion of cases. This means attempts to reach the person who had tested positive had failed or they did not provide details of their contacts. Incomplete attempts made up 12.4 per cent of cases in the week ending Dec 5, nearly trebling to 35.8 per cent in the week ending Dec 26. Even among the completed cases, more than a quarter took longer than three days. Commentary Share Time for Scotland’s opposition to force the end of ‘lockdown by stealth’ Alan Cochrane This was the week that Nicola Sturgeon appeared to accept that there was more than one way to stop a pandemic surging out of control and that a programme of heavier restrictions wasn’t among them. However, if we’re to believe that this was a genuine Damascene conversion to something much more in tune with Boris Johnson’s approach in England, then the Scottish First Minister must surely abandon her insistence that she plans to keep her controls in place for another 10 days. And it is now up to what opposition there is at Holyrood to force the end of what others have called a “lockdown by stealth”. Her terminology this week suggested a change of emphasis, with my colleague, Simon Johnson, reporting that she told the Scottish Parliament she was planning a blueprint to live with the virus in the long term that would be “more proportionate and sustainable and less restrictive”. It was essentially an admission that hard-line restrictions weren’t effective anymore. Sadly, however, none of the above meant that the restrictions she’d imposed to take effect from Boxing Day, with nightclubs closed, table service only in pubs and severe limits on all gatherings, whether inside or out, would be scrapped. They’re still supposed to last until Jan 17. Unless, of course, she has another change of heart. After all, she initially said that she wouldn’t change the self-isolation rule from 10 days to seven, which the Prime Minister did for England on Dec 22 when everyone in Scotland – from the hospitality industry to public services, all stretched by staff shortages, were pleading with her to follow suit. In an incredible explanation, she insisted that she had to adhere to advice from her government’s advisers, while Mr Johnson listened to his experts – plainly ignoring the fact that many in both groups were the same people. Then – and for no other reason than fear of being seen to be “copying Boris” – she refused to budge even to the extent of telling Holyrood on Dec 29 that she’d think about it “in a few days”. And so, this week, she did what she should have done two weeks ago and reduced the quarantine period to seven days. Also in the past week – but a day after it had been announced in London – her government abandoned the requirement for airport passenger checks, with Humza Yosaf, her hapless health minister, complaining about England’s “unilateral” behaviour on the issue. Ms Sturgeon has her first opportunity to revisit things in four days’ time when she delivers her Covid update to Holyrood. The huge increase in cases caused by the omicron variant is still causing major problems in Scotland – Army personnel have been called in to assist medical teams in Grampian and an additional 500 special police officers and trainees are being drafted in to fill vacancies in forces all over the country. But there are clear signs that while it is more transmissible, omicron is causing much less serious illness and leads to fewer hospital admissions. Figures released yesterday revealed that only one in a hundred people who catch Covid require hospital care following the UK’s vaccination programme, with Public Health Scotland reporting that the proportion of people who need hospital care after getting the virus dropped from 12 per cent in January last year to 1 per cent in December. The study also found that four in 10 people in hospital with Covid were being treated for other conditions, rather than requiring medical care for the virus. An urgent rethink of Scotland’s remaining Covid restrictions is necessary and it is up to opposition politicians to force a change in the coming days. Coronavirus Share Strict Welsh curbs fail to stem surge in cases Drakeford calls England ‘global outlier’ despite infections in Principality rising three times faster India McTaggart Alex Clark COVID case rates in Wales are rising almost three times faster than those in England despite tougher restrictions, the latest figures show. People in Wales have been living under alert-level-two measures – including mandatory face coverings indoors, a six-person limit for meeting in public places and the closure of nightclubs – since Boxing Day. Despite the measures, the country’s Covid cases have almost doubled since Dec 26, with an increase of 94 per cent, according to government data. England’s cases have increased by 34 per cent. Under England’s Plan B measures – less strict than in Wales – people have been told to work from home where possible, wear face coverings on public transport and in public places and show proof of Covid vaccination status to access large events and nightclubs. Prof Robert Dingwall, a former government Covid adviser, from Nottingham Trent University, said the omicron variant in Wales was “driving an increase which is not really being contained by these extra restrictions”. He said: “All of the extra interventions put in place by the Welsh Government really do not seem to have had any impact.” He added that the same scenario is taking place in certain places in France “which have a lot more restrictions, but are also having big waves of Covid, especially in the major cities”. “Omicron is so infectious that actually nothing you do makes much difference,” he said. It came as Mark Drakeford, the Welsh First Minister, confirmed yesterday that alert-level-two measures would remain for at least one more week, with case rates “rising steeply”. “Cases are far higher now than they were at the peak of all previous waves,” Mr Drakeford said as he warned that the “peak” of the wave could be another 10 to 14 days away. “Omicron is now the dominant form of the virus in Wales and cases are rising rapidly,” he said, adding that previous Covid waves “are nothing compared to the size and speed” of the variant. At a press conference Mr Drakeford said England was a “global outlier” in its response to omicron and accused the Government of being “politically paralysed”. He said the Prime Minister “is unable to secure an agreement through his Cabinet to take the actions that his advisers have been telling him ought to have been taken”. Official figures show there are more than 2,300 cases per 100,000 people across Wales, compared with 1,271 across England. supplementary_news.content: Get all your news in one place. 100's of premium titles. One app. Start reading Get all your news in one place. 100's of premium titles. One news app. Start reading Medical Daily Cole Mercer Aug 25, 2026, 4:00 PM COVID at Delivery Was Tied to Higher Preterm Birth and ICU Risk in 2.6 Million Hospitalizations Covid-19 Pregnancy Omicron United States The Analysis and Its Measurements A retrospective analysis of nearly 2.6 million United States delivery hospitalizations found that patients diagnosed with COVID-19 at the time of delivery were more likely to be admitted to intensive care and more likely to deliver preterm than those without a COVID diagnosis. The study, published in PLOS One , examined 2,561,615 delivery-related hospital discharges between April 1, 2020, and March 31, 2023. Of those, 53,226, or about 2.1 percent, carried a COVID-19 diagnosis. Researchers led by investigators at the US Department of Health and Human Services compared outcomes across four variant periods: pre-Alpha, Alpha, Delta, and the first Omicron wave. The elevated risk of maternal ICU admission and preterm birth held across the full pandemic period. Risk of fetal death at 20 weeks or later was elevated during the pre-Alpha and Delta periods specifically. Cesarean delivery rates rose during the study window with the exception of the Alpha and first Omicron periods, according to CIDRAP's report on the paper. The authors framed the central finding as one about variability rather than magnitude, writing that "obstetric risk associated with COVID-19 was not static but evolved" across variant periods, and describing the results as a framework for assessing variant-driven shifts in pregnancy risk during future outbreaks. The Delta Period Is Where the Signal Concentrates The variant breakdown is the part of this study that adds something new, and it is also the part most likely to be flattened in coverage. Prior research established that COVID in pregnancy carries an elevated risk. This analysis shows that the size of that risk varied substantially depending on which virus was circulating. Delta shows the most severe effects. That is consistent with what was observed in the general population during that period, when Delta produced more severe illness than either the earlier strains or Omicron. That pattern warrants caution in how anyone reads the headline. A finding averaged from 2020 through early 2023 is not a statement about the risk posed by the variants circulating now. Neither the virus nor the population is the same. Vaccination coverage among pregnant people changed dramatically over the study window, prior infection was near-universal by the end of the window, and treatment options expanded. A single pooled risk estimate would obscure all of that, which is precisely why the authors split the analysis by period. Fetal death at 20 weeks or later is the most serious outcome examined, and its elevation was confined to two of the four periods rather than running throughout. Reporting it as a general finding of the study would overstate what was observed. Association Here Is Not a Causal Verdict This is a retrospective cohort study based on hospital administrative records, and the design has limitations that should be presented alongside the results rather than after them. A COVID-19 diagnosis code at delivery indicates a recorded infection, not necessarily a symptomatic one, and not necessarily one that caused anything. Some preterm births in the COVID group were likely medically induced because clinicians decided delivery was safer than continuing the pregnancy in a sick patient, which is a clinical decision rather than a direct biological effect. Others may have been spontaneous. Administrative data generally cannot separate the two. The researchers controlled for a broad set of maternal risk factors, which strengthens the analysis without converting it into proof of causation. Testing practices also varied across the period, with universal screening at delivery common in some hospitals and at some times but not others, which affects who lands in the COVID group at all. The authors themselves position the work as corroborating prior findings rather than establishing something new about the mechanism. That is an appropriate description, and it is a meaningful contribution: consistent results at this scale make the underlying association harder to dismiss as an artifact of small samples or single-center practice. The Practical Reading for People Who Are Pregnant Now The practical takeaway is narrower and calmer than the numbers might suggest. Nothing here changes clinical guidance. Professional guidance has treated pregnancy as a risk factor for severe COVID-19 since early in the pandemic, and this analysis is consistent with that position rather than a departure from it. Anyone who is pregnant and has questions about COVID vaccination, testing, or what to do if they develop symptoms should raise them with their obstetric clinician, who can weigh individual history alongside other prenatal decisions such as maternal immunization against other viruses . The findings are not a reason for alarm about a current pregnancy. They describe outcomes among people infected during earlier phases of the pandemic, in a different immunological and clinical environment. They do not forecast what infection would mean today. What the study does support is a systems argument. The authors call for ongoing maternal health surveillance and adaptive healthcare policies, and their point is that pregnancy risk from a respiratory pathogen can shift materially within months as a virus changes. That has implications for how hospitals staff obstetric units and how quickly guidance is revised during the next outbreak, which is a different conversation from what any individual patient should do this week. It also depends on surveillance holding up, and MedicalDaily has reported that national COVID monitoring has thinned even as test positivity climbed this summer. Several questions remain open. The analysis cannot say how much of the preterm birth signal reflects medically indicated delivery versus spontaneous labor. It does not report vaccination status, so it cannot describe how much protection vaccination provided in this population, a gap that matters given how unevenly COVID vaccination has been distributed across demographic groups . And it ends in March 2023, leaving the more recent variant periods unexamined. Whether later variants track the Omicron pattern or the Delta one is not something this study can answer. Key Questions Answered What did the study find? Among 2,561,615 US delivery hospitalizations from April 2020 through March 2023, a COVID-19 diagnosis at delivery was associated with higher rates of maternal ICU admission and preterm birth throughout the period studied. How many patients had COVID? 53,226, or about 2.1 percent of the delivery discharges examined. Was fetal death elevated? Risk of fetal death at 20 weeks or later was elevated during the pre-Alpha and Delta periods, not across all four variant periods. Does this prove COVID caused these outcomes? No. This is a retrospective cohort study using hospital administrative records. It shows association after adjustment for maternal risk factors, not causation. Does it apply to variants circulating now? Not directly. The data ends in March 2023. Population immunity, vaccination coverage, and the virus itself have all changed since. Does clinical guidance change? No. Pregnancy has been recognized as a risk factor for severe COVID-19 since early in the pandemic, and these findings are consistent with existing guidance. What should someone who is pregnant do? Discuss COVID vaccination, testing, and a symptom plan with an obstetric clinician who knows their history. supplementary_news.content_title: COVID Brain Fog May Not Be Irreversible
supplementary_news.content: The acute medical emergency presented by the COVID-19 pandemic might be over, but we’re still living with the fallout. For millions of people that means a lingering and frustrating “brain fog” clouding their cognitive abilities. The original virus and two subsequent variants (Alpha and Delta) proved to be particularly cruel in that regard, but the Omicron variant was a little milder. In fact, a new study published in the journal Neuroprotection shows cognitive damage done by Omicron wasn’t irreversible for everyone. A team of neurologists followed more than 2,000 patients hospitalized with COVID-19 during the Omicron wave in China from December 2022 until March 2023). To determine how their mental health fared, researchers phoned the participants to administer cognitive tests six months and two years after their discharge date. They found some pretty good news. Two-third of the patients showed no decline in their mental faculties at all, and nearly a quarter (22 percent) experienced reversible cognitive decline. This group’s cognitive assessment scores rose an average of three points (out of a possible 40) thanks to improvements in attention and calculation, learning ability, executive function, and more. Read more: “Long COVID Leaves Clues in the Blood” “Our findings indicate that cognitive decline after Omicron infection is not necessarily permanent,” study author Yan Wan of the Huazhong University of Science and Technology explained in a statement . “The substantial recovery observed over two years is encouraging, but the persistence of deficits in a vulnerable minority shows why patients at higher risk should not be overlooked.” That’s the bad news. Roughly 11 percent of the participants experienced irreversible decline, and for over a third of those, the condition was progressive. This sliver of Omicron patients showed a four-point decrease in the cognitive assessments. What makes these unlucky few so vulnerable? Longer hospital stays, more severe COVID, and high blood pressure, to name a few factors. The researchers also found that those 60 or older had four times the risk of suffering progressive decline, with each subsequent COVID infection increasing that risk twofold. More education and vaccinations, however, showed some protective benefits. According to the team, these findings could lead to better care and prevention of post-COVID brain fog. “Our results support a more targeted approach to long-term cognitive care after COVID-19,” study author Bo Hu of the Huazhong University of Science and Technology said. “Identifying high-risk patients early could help guide monitoring and rehabilitation, while broader prevention measures such as vaccination may reduce the likelihood of progressive decline.” In the almost seven years since the first infection, COVID-19 has made the shift from pandemic to endemic. Our treatment strategies will have to adjust accordingly. Enjoying Nautilus ? Subscribe to our free newsletter .
